title: Resource Allocation and Stage Checks: A Reading and Listening Practice Test
instructions: 本材料为模拟练习材料，不是官方雅思考试，也不代表任何官方分数。阅读部分包含三篇带标题的文章，共40题（第1–13题对应第一篇，第14–26题对应第二篇，第27–40题对应第三篇）；听力部分包含四个部分，每部分10题，共40题。请按题目顺序作答。所有填空题的答案必须与原文完全一致，且不超过题目规定的字数。判断题（True/False/Not Given）请根据原文选择：True（原文明确支持）、False（原文明确矛盾）、Not Given（原文未提供所需信息）。选择题请选择最佳答案。所有数据与场景均为原创模拟内容。

Passage 1: The Riverside Allotment Scheme

A. Six years ago, the town of Marlow-on-Sea turned a neglected strip of land beside the old railway line into a community allotment scheme. The land had been used for storing building materials, and the council had received complaints about rubbish and weeds for almost a decade. A local teacher, Priya Nair, suggested that the space could grow vegetables for families who lived in flats without gardens. The council agreed to lease the land to a volunteer group for a symbolic rent of one pound per year, on the condition that the group maintained the fences and kept the site tidy. The scheme now has thirty plots, each roughly twelve square metres, and a waiting list of more than forty households.

B. The scheme is run by a committee of seven volunteers, including Priya, a retired engineer called Tom Beckett, and a secondary-school student named Aisha Rahman. The committee meets on the first Tuesday of every month in the back room of the Sea View Café. At these meetings the members review how the plots are being used, decide how to spend the small income from plot fees, and plan work days when everyone helps to repair paths or clear weeds. Tom keeps the accounts in a simple notebook, and Aisha manages the scheme's social media page, which now has over nine hundred followers. According to Priya, the most difficult part of the committee's work is not growing vegetables but deciding fairly how to share limited resources such as water, compost and tools.

C. Water is the scheme's most serious constraint. There is no mains supply on the site, so gardeners collect rainwater in six large tanks that were donated by a local business. In a normal summer this is enough, but in a dry summer the tanks empty quickly. Two years ago, during a heatwave that lasted five weeks, the committee had to introduce a rota: each household could water only on two evenings per week, and only between seven and nine o'clock. Some gardeners complained that their tomatoes suffered, but most accepted the rule because they could see that without it the tanks would have run dry within a fortnight. The committee is now applying for a grant to install a second set of tanks and a simple drip-irrigation system, which would use water more efficiently.

D. Tools and compost are shared according to a similar principle. The scheme owns about forty hand tools, which are stored in a locked shed near the main gate. Any member can borrow a tool by writing their name and the date in a logbook, and tools must be returned clean within three days. This system works well in spring, when demand is highest, but the committee has noticed that in autumn several tools go missing or are returned damaged. Tom has proposed that each member should pay a small deposit of five pounds, which would be returned at the end of the year if all borrowed items have been accounted for. The committee has not yet voted on this proposal, because some members feel it would discourage the poorest households from joining.

E. Compost is produced on site from kitchen waste and grass cuttings. There are three compost bays, and members are asked to add material in the correct proportions: roughly two parts dry material, such as leaves and cardboard, to one part green material, such as vegetable peelings. Last year the committee discovered that too much green material had been added to one bay, and the result was a wet, smelly heap that attracted flies. Since then, Priya has run two short workshops on composting, and the quality of the compost has improved noticeably. The scheme now produces enough compost to supply every plot, which saves members money and reduces the amount of waste sent to landfill.

F. The committee carries out a formal review, or stage check, at the end of each growing season, in October. At this review the members compare what they planned in spring with what actually happened. They look at three measures: how many plots were cultivated for the whole season, how much water was used, and how many members attended work days. Last October the figures showed that twenty-six of the thirty plots had been cultivated continuously, that water use had fallen by about fifteen per cent compared with the previous year, and that attendance at work days had dropped sharply. The committee concluded that the drop in attendance was partly because work days had been scheduled on Sundays, when many members were busy with family commitments. As a result, the committee decided to move work days to Saturday mornings and to send reminders by text message two days in advance.

G. Looking ahead, the scheme faces a familiar problem: demand for plots is far higher than supply. The committee has identified a further strip of unused land behind the compost bays, which could accommodate perhaps ten more plots. However, extending the site would require new fencing, a second water tank and, most importantly, more volunteers to manage the additional administration. Priya has warned that if the scheme grows too quickly, the committee may not be able to maintain the quality of the site, and the council might withdraw its support. The committee has therefore agreed to expand slowly, adding five plots each year, and to review the decision at each October meeting.

Passage 2: Budget Choices at Northgate College Library

A. Northgate College is a further-education college with about 2,400 students, most of whom are between sixteen and nineteen years old. Its library occupies the ground floor of the main building and has an annual budget of £48,000, which is set by the college's finance committee each spring. The library manager, Daniel Okafor, is responsible for deciding how this money is divided between printed books, digital subscriptions, periodicals, furniture and staff training. He describes the budget as 'a set of difficult choices rather than a single decision', because spending more on one category always means spending less on another.

B. Three years ago, the library spent almost two-thirds of its budget on printed books. Daniel became concerned that this balance no longer matched how students actually studied. He analysed the library's borrowing records and found that borrowing of printed books had fallen by about a third over five years, while the number of logins to the library's online databases had more than doubled. He also ran a short survey of four hundred students. The results showed that fifty-eight per cent of students used digital resources for most of their research, twenty-seven per cent preferred printed books, and the remaining fifteen per cent said they used both equally. Daniel presented these findings to the finance committee, which agreed to a gradual change rather than a sudden one.

C. The current budget reflects this compromise. Printed books now receive £14,000, down from £30,000 three years ago, while digital subscriptions receive £18,000, up from £7,000. Periodicals, such as magazines and academic journals, receive £6,000. Furniture and equipment receive £5,000, and staff training receives £2,000. The remaining £3,000 is kept as a contingency fund for unexpected costs, such as replacing a broken computer or paying for an urgent repair. Daniel argues that the contingency fund is essential: in his first year as manager, a leak in the roof damaged several shelves of books, and without reserve money the library would have had to cancel new purchases for a whole term.

D. Digital subscriptions bring particular challenges because most of them are annual contracts that renew automatically. If the library cancels a subscription, students lose access to the resource immediately, and some contracts require notice three months before the renewal date. Daniel therefore keeps a detailed calendar showing when each subscription must be reviewed. He also checks usage statistics every term. Last year he discovered that one online encyclopedia, which cost £4,500 a year, had been accessed only forty times in twelve months. He cancelled it and used the money to extend a more popular resource, an academic journal collection, which is now used by over six hundred students each month.

E. Printed books, by contrast, are bought once and remain on the shelves for years, but they take up space and become out of date. The library has limited shelving, and Daniel has introduced a policy of withdrawing books that have not been borrowed for five years. Last year about nine hundred books were removed from the shelves; some were sold to students at a small price, and others were donated to a charity. This policy has freed space for a new quiet study area with twenty desks, which students requested repeatedly in the survey. Daniel notes that the quiet area has become one of the most heavily used parts of the library, even though it does not appear as a separate item in the budget.

F. The library's stage checks take place at the end of each term, in December, March and June. At each check, Daniel and his two assistants compare actual spending with the planned budget and review a small set of performance measures. These include the number of books borrowed, the number of database logins, attendance at study-skills workshops, and student satisfaction, which is measured by a short questionnaire. In the December check last year, the team noticed that spending on periodicals was running ahead of plan because the price of several journals had risen unexpectedly. They responded by cancelling two journals that were rarely read and by asking the college to negotiate a group discount with the publisher. By the March check, periodical spending was back within the planned figure.

G. Daniel believes that the most valuable part of the stage check is not the numbers themselves but the conversation they prompt. 'A budget tells you what you planned,' he says, 'but a review tells you what actually happened and why.' He gives an example from two years ago, when the library had spent a large sum on a new set of reference books that students hardly used. The review revealed that the books had been chosen by staff without consulting students. Since then, the library has invited a small group of students to comment on proposed purchases before orders are placed. Daniel admits that this slows down the buying process, but he argues that it has reduced waste and improved trust between students and staff.

H. Looking ahead, Daniel expects the pressure on the budget to continue. The college plans to increase student numbers by about ten per cent over the next three years, which will increase demand for both study space and digital resources. He has proposed that the library should move towards a 'core plus flexible' model: a core of essential subscriptions and a basic printed collection, protected in the budget, plus a flexible portion that can be redirected each year according to usage data. The finance committee has asked him to present a detailed plan at its next meeting in May.

Passage 3: Planning a Dissertation: A Student's Guide to Resources and Reviews

A. For many students, the dissertation is the largest piece of work they will ever complete. It requires sustained effort over several months, and it is easy to lose direction without a clear plan. This guide explains two connected ideas that can help: resource allocation, which means deciding in advance how to use your limited time, money and energy, and stage checks, which means stopping at regular intervals to review what you have done and to adjust your plan. Neither idea is complicated, but both are frequently neglected.

B. The first task is to break the dissertation into stages. A typical dissertation might be divided into reading and note-taking, designing the method, collecting data, analysing results, writing the first draft, and revising. Each stage should have a deadline, and each deadline should be realistic. A common mistake is to estimate how long a stage will take in the best possible circumstances. If you think the reading stage will take three weeks, it is wiser to allow four, because unexpected problems, such as a book arriving late through an interlibrary loan, are almost certain to occur. The extra time is often called a buffer, and it is not laziness; it is planning for reality.

C. The second task is to allocate your resources honestly. Time is the resource students most often misjudge. If you have a part-time job, a caring responsibility or a long commute, those hours are not available for study, and pretending otherwise will only create stress later. Write down the hours you genuinely have each week and divide them between your stages. Money is a second resource: you may need to pay for software, printing, travel to archives or participant rewards. Set a limit for each category before you begin, and keep receipts. Energy is the third resource, and it is the one most often ignored. Most people cannot write well for eight hours a day; two or three focused hours may produce more than a whole distracted afternoon.

D. If you are working in a group, allocation becomes a matter of fairness as well as efficiency. Divide tasks according to skills and interests rather than simply splitting the work equally. One member may be skilled at statistical analysis, another at interviewing, and a third at editing. However, skill-based division can create problems if one person's task depends on another's. If the analyst cannot begin until the interviewers have finished, then the interviewers' deadline becomes critical for the whole group. A simple chart showing who does what and when each task must be finished can prevent most misunderstandings. It is also wise to agree in writing what will happen if someone falls behind.

E. Stage checks turn a plan into a working system. At the end of each stage, set aside an hour to answer four questions. First, did I complete what I planned? Second, if not, why not? Third, what does this tell me about my estimates for the remaining stages? Fourth, what will I change? The third question is the most important and the most often skipped. If your reading stage took five weeks instead of four, you should not simply feel guilty; you should revise your estimate for the writing stage, which may also take longer than you expected. A stage check is a tool for learning, not a trial.

F. It is useful to record the answers to these questions in a short written log. A log of half a page per stage is enough. Over time, the log reveals patterns that are invisible in the moment: perhaps you consistently underestimate the time needed for writing, or you consistently lose a week when other coursework deadlines cluster together. Once you can see a pattern, you can plan around it. Many students find that after two or three stage checks their estimates become noticeably more accurate, simply because they have evidence to base them on rather than optimism.

G. Communication should run alongside the checks. If you are falling behind, tell your supervisor or your group early, not at the final deadline. Supervisors can often suggest ways to narrow the scope of a project, and they may know of resources you have not considered. Group members can redistribute tasks if they are told in time. Waiting until the last minute removes these options and turns a manageable problem into a crisis. A short email at the end of each stage, summarising what you have done and what you plan next, takes ten minutes and prevents most difficulties.

H. Finally, be prepared to reduce the scope of your work. Many students begin with an ambitious plan and then feel that reducing it is a failure. In practice, a smaller project completed thoroughly is usually marked more highly than a large project completed badly. If your stage check shows that you cannot collect all the data you planned, it is better to analyse fewer cases in depth than to rush the analysis of everything. The purpose of resource allocation and stage checks is not to make the work smaller, but to make sure that the work you do is finished, honest and well presented.

I. In summary, plan your stages, estimate generously, allocate your time, money and energy honestly, review your progress at the end of each stage, keep a short log, communicate early, and be willing to adjust the scope. These habits will not guarantee a perfect dissertation, but they will make the process calmer and the result stronger.
transcript:
Section 1: Social Dialogue (a conversation at the allotment site)

Woman: Hello, are you here about the waiting list for a plot?
Man: Yes, I am. I phoned last month, but I haven't heard anything since.
Woman: Let me check. What's your name?
Man: It's Owen Marsh. M-A-R-S-H.
Woman: Ah yes, here you are. You're number twelve on the list. Sorry, I said eleven earlier, didn't I? No, it's twelve.
Man: Twelve. And how long do people usually wait?
Woman: It varies. Last year it was about eight months, but now it's closer to a year, I'm afraid.
Man: A year. That's longer than I expected.
Woman: I know. The problem is that we only have thirty plots and nobody gives one up in summer.
Man: Could I share a plot with someone in the meantime?
Woman: That's allowed, actually. Some members share. You'd need to agree it with the plot holder, and both names go in the logbook.
Man: Good. And is there anything I can do while I'm waiting?
Woman: You could come to the work days. They're on Saturday mornings now, not Sundays — we changed that in October.
Man: Saturday mornings. What time?
Woman: Nine until twelve. You don't need to be a member to help.
Man: That sounds useful. One more thing — do I need to pay anything to join the list?
Woman: No, the list is free. The fee is only when you actually get a plot, and that's twenty pounds a year.
Man: Great. Thanks very much.
Woman: You're welcome. See you on a Saturday, hopefully.

Section 2: Social Monologue (a committee announcement)

Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to the October meeting of the Riverside Allotment Scheme. I'm Tom Beckett, and I'll give the treasurer's report tonight because Priya is unwell — she sends her apologies.

First, the accounts. Our income this year was one thousand two hundred and forty pounds, mostly from plot fees, plus a small donation from the Sea View Café. Our spending was one thousand and ninety pounds. That leaves a balance of one hundred and fifty pounds, which is lower than last year, mainly because we replaced the lock on the tool shed and bought two new water butts.

Second, the water rota. I know some of you were unhappy about the two-evening rule in July. The committee discussed it again last week and agreed to keep the rule next summer, but we will review it in May rather than waiting until July. If the new tanks are installed before June, we may be able to relax it.

Third, the tool deposit. We didn't vote on it tonight because three members were absent. We'll vote at the November meeting instead. Please read the proposal on the noticeboard before then.

Fourth, work days. As you know, we moved them from Sunday to Saturday morning. Attendance has improved — twenty-two people came to the last one, compared with nine in September. Thank you to everyone who helped clear the path.

Finally, a reminder that the compost workshop is on the second Saturday of next month at ten o'clock, not eleven as it says on the old poster. Priya will run it. Please bring gloves.

Section 3: Academic Discussion (a tutorial about a college library project)

Tutor: Come in, Mei. So, you wanted to talk about your project on library budgets.
Student: Yes. I've chosen Northgate College, and I've got their figures for three years.
Tutor: Good. What have you found so far?
Student: Well, the biggest change is digital subscriptions. They went from seven thousand pounds to eighteen thousand.
Tutor: That's a big shift. Did the college cut printed books by the same amount?
Student: Not exactly. Printed books went from thirty thousand to fourteen thousand, so that's a cut of sixteen thousand, which is actually more than the increase in digital.
Tutor: Interesting. So where did the rest of the money go?
Student: Some went to the contingency fund, and some to furniture and training. Oh — and they cancelled one encyclopedia that cost four and a half thousand a year.
Tutor: How did they decide to cancel it?
Student: They looked at usage. It had only been accessed forty times in a year.
Tutor: Right. Now, be careful with that kind of figure. Forty accesses doesn't necessarily mean the resource was useless — it might have been used by a small number of researchers very intensively.
Student: That's a fair point. I hadn't thought of that. I'll mention it as a limitation.
Tutor: Good. And how are you organising the project itself?
Student: I've divided it into four stages, and I'm doing a check at the end of each one. I've just finished the data collection stage.
Tutor: And did it take as long as you planned?
Student: No, it took two weeks longer, because the college took a while to send the second year's figures.
Tutor: So what will you change?
Student: I've added a week to the writing stage, and I'm going to start drafting the method section now rather than waiting.
Tutor: That sounds sensible. Send me a short summary after your next check.

Section 4: Academic Lecture (resource allocation and stage checks in project management)

Good morning. Today I want to examine two ideas that are often treated as separate but are in fact closely connected: resource allocation and stage checks. My argument is that a stage check is not simply a report on the past; it is the mechanism by which resources are reallocated during a project.

Let me begin with a definition. Resource allocation is the process of deciding how limited inputs — time, money, people and equipment — are distributed across the tasks of a project. In theory, this is done once, at the planning stage. In practice, it must be done repeatedly, because the information available at the start of a project is always incomplete. A team that allocates all its resources at the beginning and never revisits the decision is not being efficient; it is being inflexible.

This is where stage checks become important. A stage check is a scheduled review at the end of a phase, in which the team compares planned progress with actual progress and decides what to change. There are three features that distinguish an effective stage check from a merely formal one.

First, it must be scheduled in advance. Reviews that happen only when something goes wrong tend to be rushed and defensive. A review that is in the calendar from the start is treated as normal, and people are more willing to report problems honestly.

Second, it must use measures that were agreed before the phase began. If a team invents new criteria at the review, the exercise becomes a negotiation about whose standards count rather than a learning process. In the library example we discussed earlier, the measures — borrowing, logins, attendance, satisfaction — were fixed in advance, which made the December review straightforward.

Third, and most importantly, a stage check must have the authority to change the plan. A review that produces a report but no decision is wasted effort. If the review shows that a task is taking longer than expected, the team must be able to move resources, reduce scope or extend a deadline. This is why I said at the beginning that the two ideas are connected: the stage check is the moment at which allocation actually happens.

Now, there are common objections. Some managers argue that stage checks slow projects down. In my experience, the opposite is usually true. A project without checks tends to discover its problems at the end, when there is no time left to solve them. Others argue that checks create blame. This depends entirely on how they are run. If the purpose of the review is to identify what went wrong and who is responsible, people will hide information. If the purpose is to identify what the plan got wrong, people will share it.

Let me give one brief example from a simulated case study. A small team was building an online course. At the first stage check, they found that the video production stage had used sixty per cent of its budget but completed only thirty per cent of the lessons. The team had two options: reduce the number of videos, or simplify the format. They chose to simplify the format, which allowed them to finish all the lessons within the original budget. Notice that the decision was possible only because the check happened early enough to act on.

To conclude, resource allocation without stage checks is a plan that cannot adapt, and stage checks without the power to reallocate are a ritual without effect. The two must be designed together. Thank you. I'm happy to take questions.

grammar.title: 条件句；数量词；段落间的指代与衔接
grammar.explanation: 条件句表示“如果……就……”。真实条件句：if从句用一般现在时，主句用will/can等（如If the scheme grows too quickly, the committee may not be able to maintain the quality）。虚拟条件句：if从句用一般过去时，主句用would/could + 动词原形，表示与现在事实相反（如If I had more time, I would join）。数量词如some, any, many, much, a few, a little, several, enough用来表示不确定的数量，注意可数名词与不可数名词的搭配。段落间的指代与衔接依靠代词（it, they, this, these）和连接词（however, therefore, for example, as a result）把前后句和段落连起来，使文章连贯。
grammar.example: If the scheme grows too quickly, the committee may not be able to maintain the quality of the site

questions.prompt: If the new tanks _____ installed before June, the committee may relax the water rule.
answers: are
questions.explanation: 真实条件句中，if从句用一般现在时表示将来，主句用may + 动词原形。
questions.evidence: If the new tanks are installed before June, we may be able to relax it.

questions.prompt: There are _____ hand tools in the shed, so members usually share them.
answers: several
questions.explanation: hand tools是可数名词复数，用several表示“几个”。
questions.evidence: The scheme owns about forty hand tools

questions.prompt: The library cancelled the encyclopedia. _____, it used the money to extend a journal collection.
answers: Instead
questions.explanation: 前后是替代关系：取消一个资源，转而用这笔钱扩展另一个资源，因此用Instead。
questions.evidence: He cancelled it and used the money to extend a more popular resource

questions.prompt: If I _____ the figures earlier, I would have changed my plan.

questions.explanation: 与过去事实相反的虚拟条件句中，if从句用had + 过去分词，主句用would have + 过去分词。
questions.evidence: If your stage check shows that you cannot collect all the data you planned, it is better to analyse fewer cases in depth
